title: The prayer at the foundations
hook: Ibrahim and Isma'il pray for a messenger from among the people (2:127–129)
carry: pray for the ones not born
tomorrow: What will you worship after me

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibrahim tested, and your line, tested, then trusted. Did you finish the hard duty, or take its last step? Today, Ibrahim again, with stones in his hands. Day three hundred forty-four.

Old buildings sometimes have a time capsule sealed into a cornerstone: a newspaper, a few coins, a letter addressed to whoever opens it in a hundred years. The builders will never meet that reader. They write anyway. In al-Baqarah, a father and son are raising the foundations of a house in a dry valley in Arabia. As they lift the stones, they speak, and much of what they say is for people who don't exist yet. Today: the prayer at the foundations.
screen: `A LETTER IN THE CORNERSTONE.` → `A FATHER AND SON, LIFTING STONES.` → `WORDS FOR PEOPLE NOT YET BORN.`

segments.voice: Last year you watched Ibrahim and Isma'il raise the Kaaba. This year, listen to what they were saying while they did it. Verse one hundred twenty-seven, in Pickthall's words: “Our Lord! Accept from us (this duty). Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Hearer, the Knower.” They're building God's house, and their first words ask that it be accepted, as if it might not be. Then the prayer grows. Make us both submissive to You, they ask, and from our descendants a nation submissive to You. Show us our rites, and turn to us. And then, in verse one hundred twenty-nine, the furthest request: Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves, who will recite Your verses to them, teach them the book and wisdom, and purify them. Consider the distance in that prayer. Muslims hold that it was answered long after, in the same valley, in Mecca, with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. A report in the Musnad of Ahmad has him say: I am the answer to the prayer of my father Ibrahim, and the good news of Isa. Notice the order inside the prayer, too. Accept what we did. Make us good. Make our children good. Send them a teacher. It moves outward, from the two of them to people they'd never see. The stones they lifted can't be pointed to today. The prayer is still read, in this surah, every day. Pray for the ones not born.
screen: `OUR LORD! ACCEPT FROM US` · `FROM US, TO OUR DESCENDANTS` · `A MESSENGER FROM AMONG THEM` · `I AM THE ANSWER TO IBRAHIM'S PRAYER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those who come after you. Think of people you'll never meet, or barely will: grandchildren, your students' students, whoever lives in your home after you, a child born this year somewhere far away. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can use the builders' own first words, Our Lord, accept from us, and then ask good for them in your own words. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Kaaba. The house Ibrahim and Isma'il raised in Mecca, praying as they built it for descendants and a messenger not yet born. Today's word.
Your line: pray for the ones not born. Today, do one thing whose good you won't see: plant something, save something, teach something. Day three hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 344 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT WILL YOU WORSHIP AFTER ME.`

howItsDone: Muslims often recite Ibrahim and Isma'il's words, Rabbana taqabbal minna, our Lord, accept from us, after completing a good deed, and pray for their children and for generations to come.

fork.setup: you and your son have just raised the foundations of God's house. what are your first words?
fork.reveal: accept from us: they ask for acceptance, as if the work might not be enough, then pray outward to their descendants.

original.note: Arabic: our Lord, accept from us; the builders' first words in 2:127.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about building the Kaaba.
what it means: a prayer said while building, reaching out to people not yet born.
what a scholar hears: the prayer of 2:129, a messenger who recites, teaches the book and wisdom, and purifies, which Muslims hold was answered in Muhammad, as the hadith in Ahmad says.
recall: saying we believe, hearts not following
peace, a greeting that is also a wish

notes: Pickthall's 2:127 quoted as used in year one; please confirm.
The hadith 'I am the answer to the prayer of Ibrahim and the glad tidings of Isa' (Musnad Ahmad, from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah and others) cited without number; confirm and grade.
'Thousands of years later' follows the usual understanding; the Qur'an gives no date for Ibrahim.
Year one (day 42) covered the building of the House; this day focuses on the words of the prayer.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'thousands of years' (teach and trapdoor) and the unsourced claim that the original stones lie under later rebuildings; 'the scholars notice' became a plain observation; 'Think about' opener and 'many Muslims' softened.
